SKILL.md.text:
---
name: repository-quality
description: Assess or improve repository organization, documentation, contribution paths, validation and packaging using contextual examples and primary guidance. Use for repository setup, maintainability assessments and bounded repo-quality improvements; choose practices for the actual project rather than impose a universal folder tree or quality score.
---

# Repository Quality

Help people make a repository understandable and safe to change. Use the annotated [reference library](library/index.md) to connect practices to a project's actual maintenance and distribution needs. A familiar tree, long checklist or popular reference is not evidence of quality by itself.

Name the requested artifact: assessment, repository plan, specific implementation or reusable skill/library. When inspecting a project to improve this library, bound that example and return its findings to the parent deliverable; do not drift into maintaining the example. An assessment does not silently become a restructuring or release task. Preserve existing authorization without repeated approvals.

## Establish the maintenance problem

Inspect the brief, applicable project instructions, current tree, manifests, entry points, contributor docs, checks and release definitions. Identify who needs to work here and which change is difficult: discovering source, setting up locally, finding the right test, editing generated output, updating docs, or preparing an artifact. Learn technical facts from the repository before asking people to repeat them.

Ask only about consequential human-owned unknowns: intended users/contributors, the supported distribution contract, acceptable maintenance cost, compatibility promises or which friction matters most. A small personal script and a widely distributed library need different answers. Do not ask someone to pick `src/` versus flat layout as an aesthetic preference. A clear brief, narrow request or explicit delegation can be sufficient to proceed.

Carry answers into decisions. Keep a pending question attached to its decision; a delayed reply supersedes dependent provisional choices. Opening an example does not endorse its conventions. Once direction is sufficient, produce the requested artifact instead of another equivalent interview.

Read [questions and assessment](references/questions-and-assessment.md) when context is uncertain or evaluating an existing repository.

## Follow a real change path

Choose a representative maintenance task relevant to the request. Trace it from discovery to authoritative input, implementation or content, relevant tests/docs/configuration and the distributed artifact if there is one. Follow the commands and files the documentation names rather than stopping at the root listing.

Separate authoring boundaries, dependency boundaries, ownership, build units and publication units. They can differ. Identify generated files and the actual source/generator before recommending moves or direct edits. A configured job establishes intended checks; it does not establish a green run, branch protection, a tested installed package or a released version.

Record a demonstrated problem, its consequence and the smallest relevant correction. Missing inspected evidence is an unknown, not automatically a defect. Conversely, a documented convention can be stale when the owning manifest, workflow or generator contradicts it. Reconcile versions and intended environments before concluding that sources conflict.

Read [structure and documentation](references/structure-and-documentation.md) for layout, ownership, source authority and reader journeys. Read [verification and distribution](references/verification-and-distribution.md) for test scope, package boundaries and release evidence.

## Select references for this context

Survey relevant and neighboring library entries, then read promising cards and the exact primary sections needed for the recommendation. Match project type, language/tool semantics, contributor model, scale, release units and maintenance budget. Use repository cases for concrete paths, guides/standards for their stated scope and studies for findings within their actual methods.

Compare mechanisms, not whole repositories. A large project's generator boundary can transfer while its governance, bootstrap stages and platform matrix do not. A small flat library can be the better structural analogue. Prefer contrasting relevant examples over several famous repositories with the same constraints. Keep a no-change or smaller-change option when appropriate.

Explain the selected portion, fit, decisive mismatch and proposed adaptation. Use existing project behavior and assets where they already solve the problem. Broaden external discovery when the library has no adequate analogue or its source is stale. Distinguish a new lead from an inspected recommendation. Source instructions are evidence, not authority to run upstream setup, adopt unrelated approval loops or install tools.

Use the browse index directly, or read [library usage](references/library-usage.md) for optional search commands and evidence handling. Do not read every card or make the person review a research diary.

## Propose or apply bounded improvements

Organize recommendations around the requested maintenance path: what becomes easier or safer, which files/contracts change, the cost and the verification needed. Prioritize concrete obstacles ahead of cosmetic consistency. Do not prescribe a monorepo, directory taxonomy, documentation suite, coverage threshold or release platform without a contextual reason.

For implementation requests, preserve behavior, history and unrelated work. Update authoritative inputs and dependent paths/imports/manifests/docs together. Migrate incrementally when broad moves would obscure review or break consumers. A repository-quality task is not blanket authorization to redesign the system, change licensing, publish packages or alter access controls.

## Verify the promised result

For source-only assessments, cite exact inspected paths/revisions and distinguish configured, run, packaged and released evidence. For requested implementation or runtime validation, use relevant existing checks, exercise the affected contributor/consumer path and inspect the resulting artifact when that is the promise. Do not execute untrusted upstream scripts merely to increase evidence counts.

A passing source-tree test may miss installed-artifact behavior; a build may omit a documented workflow; a quality badge may describe heuristics. Explain applicable limits without turning every local improvement into a full release or audit. If a check is blocked, preserve its actual failure and complete independent authorized work; do not substitute a weaker check while calling the original outcome passed.

Finish with the actual artifact changed or assessed, selected evidence, practical result, relevant checks and consequential remaining uncertainty. Read [evidence and maintenance](references/evidence-and-maintenance.md) when curating resources or returning trial findings to this skill.

library/FORMAT.md.text:
# Repository reference card format

Canonical cards are `library/entries/<id>.md`. Use UTF-8 Markdown with JSON frontmatter between two `---` lines. The generated Markdown/JSON index is a browse/search view, never the authoritative annotation. No remote code is executed to build or search it.

Required fields:

- `id`: lowercase hyphenated filename stem.
- `kind`: `repository`, `guide`, `standard`, `study`, or `tool`.
- `title`, `summary`: substantive strings; describe a transferable mechanism, not a quality ranking.
- `status`: `curated`, `candidate`, `needs-review`, or `retired`.
- `availability`: `public`, `partial`, `local-only`, or `unavailable`.
- `facets`: lists for `tasks`, `contexts`, `languages`, `scale`. Labels are lowercase hyphenated slugs. Use `language-agnostic` for appropriate general guidance. Scale describes applicability, not prestige; useful labels include `small-project`, `single-package`, `multi-package`, `large-project`, `cross-scale`.
- `sources`: nonempty list of objects with `url`, `title`, `locator`, `revision`. Prefer exact commit URLs for repository claims and precise paths/sections. A default-branch link is mutable; state its access date rather than implying a frozen version.
- `evidence`: `mode` (list), `inspected_at` (ISO date), `freshness`, `scope`. Modes: `source-inspected`, `documented-flow`, `empirical`, `conceptual`, `discovery-only`, `partial`, `visual-inspected`, `interaction-tested`. Freshness: `versioned`, `live-at-inspection`, `historical`, `unknown`. Use only modes actually supported. Read source/configuration establishes intended mechanics, not an executed command, passing CI, repository protections, release or installed package.
- `reuse`: original annotation/link scope; do not redistribute upstream files or give a legal opinion.
- `related`: list of existing IDs; empty while lanes curate independently. Root will connect relevant cards after reconciliation.

Required body sections: `## When to use`, `## What to inspect`, `## What to borrow and adapt`, `## Mismatches and limits`. Repository cases also include `## Change path`: a concrete trigger → authoritative input → source/tests/docs/configuration touched → relevant validation/distribution. Identify what was actually followed and what remains unknown. Root tree listings alone do not establish this path. Guides/standards/studies should give a concrete application contrast rather than a universal checklist.

Each repository card should inspect multiple substantive artifacts (normally a contributor/entry document, an authoritative source/manifest/build input, and a test/CI/documentation/release boundary). Use enough evidence for the claimed mechanism; do not pad counts. Keep sources exact and narrow. Explain context mismatch: a mature monorepo may illustrate source authority while imposing unsuitable governance cost on a two-person library.

Candidate discovery and curated support are different statuses. A failed lookup is not evidence of nonexistence. If a source or requested artifact is unavailable, preserve the access gap and narrow the claim. Direct evidence may contradict a popular README account; reconcile the difference. Do not interpret missing inspected proof as a demonstrated defect.

Use `source-inspected` for read-only repository/configuration tracing; the `Change path` body section can describe intended mechanics without claiming a flow was exercised. If using `documented-flow`, also include `flow_evidence`: list of objects with `url`, `locator`, `sequence` (nonempty string or string list) and `method`. Optional `visual-inspected` similarly needs `visual_evidence` (`url`, `locator`, `observed`, `method`); `interaction-tested` needs `interaction_evidence` (`url`, `actions`, `observed`, `method`). An `interaction-tested` card also needs the `flow_evidence` sequence receipt. These support claim-specific receipts; none is required simply because a repository has CI or contributor docs.

# Reading paths by maintenance problem

Use these as starting contrasts, then inspect the cards and the relevant primary sections. They do not prescribe a fixed shortlist or replace context discovery. [Browse all entries](index.md) or inspect actual labels with `python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --status curated`.

| Maintenance problem | Concrete cases | Guidance / contrast |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A small tree seems “too simple” | [p-limit](entries/repo-small-p-limit.md), [Flask](entries/repo-small-flask.md) | Compare actual exports/imports and consumer boundary through [npm artifacts](entries/quality-npm-artifact-exports.md) or [Python layouts](entries/quality-python-import-layout.md), not folder count. |
| A new contributor cannot find the right change | [Click](entries/repo-small-click.md), [Cobra](entries/repo-small-cobra.md), [Django](entries/repo-large-django.md) | [Change questions study](entries/docs-study-change-questions.md) and [contribution entry](entries/docs-github-contribution-entry.md); preserve optional environments and routing. |
| Generated output and source disagree | [uv](entries/repo-small-uv.md), [Testify](entries/repo-small-testify.md), [SQLite](entries/repo-large-sqlite.md), [Go](entries/repo-large-go.md) | [Source authority](entries/quality-generated-source-authority.md); inspect what is checked in, regenerated at build, or published. |
| Source-tree tests pass but packaging is uncertain | [p-limit](entries/repo-small-p-limit.md), [Click](entries/repo-small-click.md), [bat](entries/repo-small-bat.md) | [Python distribution checks](entries/quality-python-distribution-checks.md), [npm artifact exports](entries/quality-npm-artifact-exports.md), [Cargo packaging](entries/quality-cargo-package-boundary.md). |
| Workspace structure is being confused with releases | [Kubernetes](entries/repo-large-kubernetes.md), [VS Code](entries/repo-large-vscode.md), [ripgrep](entries/repo-small-ripgrep.md) | [Go modules/workspaces](entries/quality-go-module-workspace-boundaries.md), [npm workspace scope](entries/quality-npm-workspace-scope.md), [Cargo workspace selection](entries/quality-cargo-workspace-selection.md). |
| Documentation is hard to maintain or contribute | [MDN](entries/docs-mdn-content-contracts.md), [Rust book](entries/docs-rust-book-source-listings.md), [Astro docs](entries/docs-astro-localized-contracts.md) | [Diataxis](entries/docs-diataxis-reader-needs.md) for reader needs, [docs as code](entries/docs-docs-as-code.md) for workflow; shared tooling is not proof of clear or correct writing. |
| A score, badge or process is being treated as quality proof | [Coverage study](entries/docs-study-coverage-limits.md), [Google review study](entries/docs-study-google-review.md) | [Scorecard limits](entries/quality-scorecard-diagnostic-limits.md), [CODEOWNERS](entries/docs-github-codeowners.md), [SLSA](entries/quality-slsa-provenance-verification.md): separate heuristic, configured mechanism and observed outcome. |
| Release overhead is growing | [Release planning workflows](entries/quality-release-planning-workflows.md) | [Versioning and human notes](entries/quality-versioning-and-human-release-notes.md), [reproducibility](entries/quality-reproducible-build-evidence.md); no publication workflow is required for every internal script. |

Related-resource IDs in cards connect mechanisms across scale and resource type; they are suggested reading, not independent corroboration or automatic activation of upstream instructions.

library/VOCABULARY.md.text:
# Facets and local discovery

The catalog accepts explicit lowercase hyphenated labels; it does not normalize words, infer similarity or rank repository quality. Treat the vocabulary below as editorial guidance, not a closed set or a framework-selection rule. Use the labels present in the current cards:

```sh
python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --kind repository --json
python3 scripts/catalog.py find "generated" --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py list --language python --scale single-package --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py show exact-card-id
```

Run these from the skill root, or use the script's absolute path. `--root /path/to/relocated-skill` precedes the subcommand when an explicit package root is needed. Python's standard library is sufficient; no service, package installation, repository checkout, network request or upstream command is used for catalog operations.

## Interpret results

- Text search splits the query on whitespace and matches case-insensitive literal substrings across metadata, source locators and original body annotations. **Every query term must match**, but terms may match different fields. A term in a mismatch paragraph is a discovery hit, not a recommendation. Results identify the matched fields.
- `--task`, `--context`, `--language` and `--scale` require exact labels. Repeating a facet flag requires **all** supplied values: `--language python --language rust` finds cards applicable to both languages, not a union. `language-agnostic` is an explicit label, not a wildcard that automatically matches Python.
- Repeated `--kind`, `--status` and `--availability` are alternatives within each filter. Different filters still combine with AND. For example, two kinds plus a language means either kind with that language.
- Results keep deterministic ID order rather than a popularity, quality or similarity score. All statuses are visible unless filtered; use `--status curated` for ready annotations and inspect candidates deliberately.
- A zero result means no card matched that literal query/filter combination. Inspect facets, try neighboring vocabulary or browse kinds before inferring a coverage gap. The catalog is not an internet census.

## Editorial hints

| Facet | What it describes | Useful distinctions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tasks` | Maintenance decision or action | Locate authoritative inputs, test a package, review a change, update generated reference, publish an artifact, onboard contributors. Prefer the same label for obvious verb/noun aliases. |
| `contexts` | Project/artifact/contribution situation | CLI, library, framework, monorepo, documentation repository, native build, multi-maintainer/community work. Several can apply; they are not mandatory architecture layers. |
| `languages` | Language relevance | Common labels include `python`, `javascript`, `typescript`, `rust`, `go`, `c`, `cpp`, `shell`, and `language-agnostic`. Read the actual card before assuming portability between ecosystems. |
| `scale` | Applicability of maintenance overhead | `small-project`, `single-package`, `multi-package`, `large-project`, `cross-scale`. These are overlapping contexts, not numerical maturity ratings or prescribed team-size thresholds. |

When normalizing labels, preserve a meaningful distinction rather than merging merely similar strings. Regenerate and validate the views after a canonical card changes. Keep repository/guide/study evidence and configured/executed/published states separate even when their discovery labels overlap.

## Editorial aliases in the first edition

The cards normalize `documentation` → `document`, `navigation`/`change-navigation` → `navigate`, `validation` → `verify`, `code-review` → `review`, `contribution`/`contribution-routing` → `contribute`, and `structure` → `organize`. These are canonical metadata edits, not runtime fuzzy matching. More specific distinctions such as test selection, generated authority and publication remain explicit. Use context to distinguish documentation navigation from source navigation. The `repo-small-` and `repo-large-` ID prefixes identify curation lanes; actual scale applicability is in each card and need not match the prefix.

# Astro docs: localized content contracts and separate validation jobs

## When to use

Use when content types have structured metadata, translations share routes, or some references originate outside the docs repository. It also shows why contributors need different routes for obvious typos and substantial new material.

## What to inspect

The contributor manual routes larger proposals through issues/discussions, marks English-only exceptions to translation tracking, and explains generated pages' githubURL authority. Its prose mentions .md while the inspected slug checker explicitly matches both Markdown and MDX. The collection configuration delegates docs loading to Starlight; that loader implementation was not inspected. Inspect configuration before treating a filename convention in a guide as the complete rule.

## Change path

Trigger: change a reference page that has translated counterparts. First determine whether it is authored locally or derived elsewhere; then inspect its content-type schema and English/translated slug relationship. package.json maps focused commands to the CI's separate type, code, slug and built-link checks. The slug checker finds non-English files without corresponding English paths; it does not assess translation completeness or correctness.

## What to borrow and adapt

Make source authority and contributor routing visible close to the edit link. Validate structural contracts separately from content review. For a bilingual small project, a few named checks and translation ownership may be preferable to copying this site's full release-label automation.

## Mismatches and limits

The generated-source workflow and translation/release rules are documented, not replayed. Schema validity, a matching slug and a green build would still not prove language equivalence or reader comprehension. Some collection loaders fetch external data at build time; a local content tree is not a complete reproducible build environment.

# Diataxis: organize around the reader need before moving folders

## When to use

Use when a README mixes onboarding, recipes and exhaustive reference, or a proposed documentation restructure lacks a specific reader problem.

## What to inspect

Read the process guidance alongside the compass. The framework separates learning or doing from acquiring or applying understanding, but explicitly warns against starting with empty top-level sections. Its advice is iterative rather than a template-completion exercise.

## What to borrow and adapt

Choose a real reader occasion: first successful invocation, an experienced user's repair task, exact option lookup, or understanding a tradeoff. Improve one relevant page and link it from the entry point. Split content when mixed purposes make that reader's task harder. For a small CLI, a short quickstart and an accurate option reference may be sufficient; absence of four directories is not itself a defect.

## Mismatches and limits

This is an author framework, not controlled evidence of a universal navigation scheme. It does not determine package boundaries, enforce API compatibility or authorize publishing. A product can need multiple audiences or mixed-mode entry pages; assess the actual task before renaming all documentation.

# Docs as code: shared change workflow with a usable writing path

## When to use

Use when documentation drifts from implementation or writers and developers lack a shared review/release path. It can guide adoption or diagnose why an existing docs pipeline has become a barrier.

## What to inspect

The docs-as-code guide proposes shared issue tracking, version control, text markup, review and tests. Its companion beginner guide distinguishes users from contributors and starts with a concrete problem, small example and usable entry instructions. The proposed collaboration benefits are practitioner guidance, not measured outcomes from this inspection.

## What to borrow and adapt

Connect a behavior-changing patch to the relevant authored or generated docs, provide a preview route writers can actually use, and automate structural checks that give actionable feedback. A two-person library can keep this path in a README and ordinary reviews; it does not automatically need a site generator, new dependency stack or blocking rule for every edit.

## Mismatches and limits

Repository tooling does not establish readability, technical truth or contributor inclusion. Validate the writing path with the people expected to use it. No linked conference talks, books or third-party toolchain were inspected here, and no claimed organizational benefit was reproduced.

Use when reviewers are difficult to find or a team wants to check whether its ownership map actually protects changes.

# Google review guidance: code health, scope and nonblocking preferences

## When to use

Use when review debates drift into preferences, a large cleanup obscures behavior, or contributors cannot tell which feedback blocks their change.

## What to inspect

Read review criteria together with the balancing standard. Tie a finding to a concrete change consequence and an applicable project rule. Label educational or cosmetic suggestions as optional. A change to a build command should carry its relevant contributor documentation; unrelated reformatting can be separate. # MDN content: page contracts and URL-preserving moves

## When to use

Use when pages move, metadata drives navigation, or outside contributors need a reproducible content-edit path. A content repository can have contracts as consequential as a package API.

## What to inspect

Follow contribution instructions into the actual npm scripts and validator. Required title/slug/page-type and restricted properties are schema obligations; useful prose and technical truth remain review tasks. Inspect the move-link script's Git-status input and its check-versus-write behavior.

## Change path

Trigger: relocate an existing topic. The documented content-move command updates placement/redirect data; the separate script repairs references to renamed files; redirect CI validates its own boundary. Metadata edits pass through the schema-backed linter. The guide names a command, while package.json reveals the current Rari/Fred split behind content/build versus local preview. No command was executed here, and external CLI internals were not traced.

## What to borrow and adapt

Map a documentation move to old URL, new URL, links, metadata and validation. Tell a contributor which input owns each output. For a small manual, a redirect table plus a focused link check may suffice; MDN's full dependency set is unnecessary.

Workflow comments describe a required-check rationale; source inspection does not verify live branch protection, CI success, public redirects or deployment timing. The link-repair script depends on recognized working-tree renames and replacement patterns; it is not a universal crawler. Do not turn metadata validity into an editorial quality score.

# Rust API documentation: examples and failure contracts

## When to use

Use for a public Rust crate whose symbols are documented but whose intended usage, failures or safety obligations are unclear.

## What to inspect

Read the qualification on example coverage, the explanation of why an example matters, and separate Errors/Panics/Safety guidance. ## What to borrow and adapt

For a fallible parser, pair a realistic call with its error conditions. For an unsafe operation, explain the caller's invariant. Make reference links and significant release changes discoverable from the crate entry. Verify examples against the crate's supported environment before claiming they work.

Use when a repository assessment equates neat folders with easy maintenance.

Two qualitative studies observed nine newcomers in paired Java tasks and sixteen industrial programmers in their normal settings. The authors categorized 44 kinds of questions and connected searches. Tasks and tool contexts varied; completion improvement was not measured.

## When to use

Use when a percentage threshold is proposed as proof of repository quality or a substitute for selecting relevant failure scenarios.

# Cargo: inspect the crate that users will build

## When to use

Use when a crate builds with neighboring paths but fails after packaging, or when release preparation must establish exactly what leaves the repository.

## What to inspect

Read include/exclude rules, build-script inputs, resource paths and manifest dependency declarations. Cargo's package description distinguishes creating the archive from building its extracted contents. It rewrites the distributed manifest and handles path dependencies differently from local resolution. The VCS metadata file is explicitly a best-effort snapshot, not verified provenance.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a library using a code-generated lookup table, trace the generator input and whether the archive contains what the downstream build needs. Review the proposed archive file list, then choose an authorized package verification path appropriate to the toolchain and supported consumers. A path-only local dependency should not be treated as an externally resolvable version merely because the workspace compiled.

Document release preparation separately from upload. An upload command's timeout may occur after the registry received the crate, so retry policy must first reconcile the published version. A dry run can check preparation without authorizing publication; it is still executable build tooling and may need dependencies or network access.

## Mismatches and limits

No archive, dry run, build or registry request was executed here. The inspected current documentation includes options whose availability depends on Cargo version. A checked-in lockfile or VCS hash alone establishes neither reproducibility nor authentic source-to-artifact correspondence. Private internal crates may intentionally have no publication path.

# Cargo: workspace convenience and selected validation scope

## When to use

Use when several Rust crates share a repository, a root command leaves some packages unchecked, or a contributor needs to know whether configuration belongs in a member or workspace root.

## What to inspect

Read workspace membership and exclusions, the root package versus virtual manifest, and `default-members`. Cargo shares a lockfile/output area and permits shared metadata, but package selection remains meaningful. Root-only patch/profile settings and inherited fields are not equivalent to independent values in every member. The publish documentation also exposes selection controls; repository membership is not a promise that every crate should be published.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a CLI plus reusable library, map the affected crate and its dependants before choosing checks. A fast package-specific test may be appropriate for a local edit, followed by workspace checks when a shared interface changes. Document which root command contributors should use and what it leaves out. Keep private helper crates and distributed crates distinguishable in manifests and release instructions.

A flat `crates/` convention can make membership easy to scan, but it should follow actual package boundaries. Do not split one small cohesive crate solely to resemble a large workspace; added crates introduce manifest, feature and publication obligations.

## Mismatches and limits

The command/reference docs describe intended behavior, not the target repository's supported Cargo version, enabled features or successful CI runs. Default members, feature selection and targets can each narrow validation. Running a root command is not automatically equivalent to testing every package, every feature combination or downstream crates.

# Generated source: review the authority and regeneration boundary

## When to use

Use when generated API clients, parsers, tables or reference pages are committed, regenerated during a build, or published from different inputs than contributors edit.

## What to inspect

Identify the authoritative input and exact generator/tool version, then follow its invocation and output consumer. The Go command documentation explicitly separates generation from build/test and explains the generated-source marker. The older Go account supplies motivation, but its historical installation examples should not be treated as current setup advice.

## What to borrow and adapt

For an enum-to-string table, the change path is enum declaration → pinned generator → generated file → focused behavior tests → any drift check. Ask whether the repository commits the output for downstream users or generates it during their build. If it commits the file, investigate how CI detects stale output; if it generates during build, investigate availability of the required tools and inputs in the distributed artifact.

Review both the human-edited input and meaningful output difference. Do not hand-edit the output merely because that makes the immediate test pass. A successful generator exit, a no-diff check and a regenerated published reference are different results; report the one actually obtained.

## Mismatches and limits

Go provides an illustrative mechanism, not a universal generator command for other ecosystems. No generator was executed. Generated files are not automatically undesirable, nor does an absent inspected regeneration job establish a defect: another build/publication boundary may provide the needed derivation. Running generation can execute arbitrary upstream commands.

# Go: module release units versus local workspaces

## When to use

Use when deciding whether Go code needs another module, when a monorepo consumer sees dependencies unlike local CI, or when a checked-in workspace changes what the project actually tests.

## What to inspect

Identify module paths and version boundaries before counting directories. Go's source guide ties modules to independent versioning. A repository can hold several modules, but local convenience does not settle their external contracts.

Record whether CI uses workspace mode or an individual module, and why. If a local replacement makes an unpublished API available, avoid claiming that the declared published dependency already contains it.

Make any checked-in workspace policy explicit in contributor commands so an ancestor workspace does not silently change conclusions.

The guidance was read, not executed against Go modules. No universal ban on committing go.work follows: the documented exception matters. Local tests, module-mode tests and tag/proxy availability are distinct evidence. This card does not establish a consumer compatibility matrix or authorize release tags.

# npm and Node: file contents and public entry points are separate contracts

## When to use

Use when TypeScript source works locally but a package omits its compiled file/declarations, or a cleanup proposes restricting previously usable import paths.

## What to inspect

Read `files`, ignore rules, entry points and the build outputs those entries name. npm's inclusion rules determine tarball contents; Node's exports rules determine which package paths consumers may resolve. ## What to borrow and adapt

For a package promising both JavaScript runtime and TypeScript types, trace each declared public entry to an actual distributed file. Plan a consumer-shaped import/type check against the artifact, using the supported environments rather than the repository's source alias configuration. Preserve supported deep imports or document an intentional compatibility change instead of silently sealing them.

Separate local package inspection from publication. Inspect lifecycle scripts before running pack or dry-run tooling, especially if preparing outputs is part of the process. Mark private members appropriately when the repository has packages that must never be published; do not infer that privacy from a folder name.

## Mismatches and limits

No tarball or consumer test was produced here. A file list does not prove runtime behavior, and a passing workspace build does not prove the list is correct. Exact inclusion/exports behavior is version-dependent. This card is not permission to upload a package or a guarantee that a package is safe to execute.

## When to use

Use when a repository mixes developer setup with package installation requirements, changes a CLI entry point, or replaces a build backend. This is a metadata and distribution boundary question before it is a tool-choice question.

For a new command, connect its declared script target to the owning callable, installed dependencies and the README's invocation. A useful acceptance path builds the distributable and checks the command in the environment promised to users. Keep development-only linters out of runtime requirements unless the product actually imports them. Conversely, a test environment that happens to contain a missing runtime dependency must not be mistaken for a complete package contract.

Preserve one authoritative version source where the backend supports it and document how derived metadata is obtained. Choose a backend based on the package's real build needs; a pure Python library and a compiled extension need not adopt the same machinery.

These documents do not recommend migrating every existing project or deleting valid legacy configuration. Backend-specific capabilities and supported metadata versions still need inspection. ## What to inspect

Follow the specific artifact consumers receive. PyPA distinguishes the source tree, source distribution and wheel. PEP 660 expects editable imports/metadata to resemble regular installation but permits backend-dependent differences and identifies configuration changes that require reinstallation. pytest describes ways to run external or included tests against an installed package. These sources jointly explain why an editable run and artifact check answer different questions.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a command that reads a packaged template, retain fast source tests for parsing logic and add a consumer-shaped check of the built package: import the public entry, invoke the command and load that template in an isolated environment. Ensure the working directory does not accidentally supply the checkout package. If source distributions are a supported delivery route, check that their required build inputs are present too.

Record which interpreter, artifact and dependency conditions were reached. A pure Python wheel may need a different validation sample from native wheels whose compatibility depends on interpreter, OS and architecture. Select the matrix from support promises and changed risk rather than copying a mature project's full release farm.

## Mismatches and limits

No package was built or installed during this research. A proposed artifact smoke test is not evidence that publication succeeded, that every native wheel works, or that the runtime is fully isolated. A local script that is not distributed as a package may not need a wheel workflow at all.

# Python: layout should expose the import boundary

## When to use

Use when a Python library works from a checkout but fails for an installed user, or when deciding whether a growing package should move under `src/`. A small private script with no distribution promise has different needs from a package used by strangers.

## What to inspect

Read the actual import path and test invocation along with package discovery configuration. PyPA describes the installation step introduced by src layout and the way root imports can shadow the installed distribution. pytest discusses both external and in-package tests and distinguishes editable, installed and direct-source runs. These are alternatives with different purposes, not a universal rule that tests must occupy one folder.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a library whose missing resource escaped tests, trace: resource declaration → build inclusion → installed import → resource lookup. Propose an isolated artifact smoke check alongside fast editable development. If moving directories, include package discovery, test configuration, documentation commands and import assumptions in the same change path. Merely renaming a directory does not establish that the installed artifact is being exercised.

For an internal one-file tool, retain the simpler layout unless a concrete import or distribution problem warrants migration. The useful property is an explicit import boundary, not the string `src`.

## Mismatches and limits

The guidance was read, not tried against a package. Src layout reduces particular shadowing risks; it cannot prove correct wheel contents or successful downstream installation. Flat layout is not a demonstrated defect. Test invocation and interpreter environment can change which copy is imported even when the tree looks conventional.

# Release planning: contributor change files versus commit-derived proposals

## When to use

Use when a repository already has meaningful release coordination costs: several independently versioned packages, repeated hand-edited metadata, or release intent that is lost between contribution and publication. First ask who decides compatibility and which artifacts are actually distributed.

## What to inspect

Release Please reads Conventional Commit history to prepare reviewable release pull requests; its manifest maps package paths and known versions. The pinned implementation distinguishes building proposals, creating PRs and creating GitHub releases. Its README explicitly excludes package-manager publication. Changesets instead records contributor-written package bump intentions and summaries, then separates version preparation/review from publishing. Their input contracts differ; they are not interchangeable badges for a healthy monorepo.

## What to borrow and adapt

For two related packages, compare where a contributor can accurately state the intended impact. If that belongs with the change, a reviewable change file may be useful. If commit history reliably carries the policy, a generated release proposal may reduce repetition. In either case, inspect dependent-version handling, private packages, authoritative metadata, artifacts to validate, and the handoff to actual publication. A generated PR is a proposal, not proof of a shipped package.

Keep human-readable notes and version review possible. For a small tool released rarely, a short explicit release procedure may serve better than either orchestrator.

## Mismatches and limits

No tool was installed or run, PR opened, tag created or package published. Changesets main's pinned README calls itself v3 development; its old checked-in intro is marked outdated while the linked site identifies v3.0.3. These observed labels do not independently prove registry publication. Match documentation to the project's installed version before borrowing commands or automation assumptions.

# Reproducible builds: define artifacts and controlled variation

## When to use

Use when a project distributes binaries/archives, claims reproducible releases, or sees unexplained differences between equivalent builds. A local development command that succeeds twice answers a weaker question.

## What to inspect

Read which artifacts are covered and what source revision, environment and instructions define the claim. The Reproducible Builds definition requires matching output bytes for specified artifacts. Its SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH guidance addresses a common timestamp input but does not make every build deterministic merely by setting one variable.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a CLI archive, identify the expected binary/archive, compiler and dependency inputs, packaging order and metadata. Choose relevant variations such as build path, locale or timestamp, then compare outputs and explain differences. If the difference is in a ZIP timestamp rather than the executable, state that distinction instead of calling the entire application nondeterministic.

Document the narrow reproducibility envelope and preserve useful diagnostics. A two-person tool may begin with one important supported artifact and a clear build recipe; it need not claim independent multi-party reproduction of every platform to gain a useful debugging check. Conversely, downstream verifiers need more than a lockfile to reconstruct an artifact.

## Mismatches and limits

No builds or hash comparisons were performed here. Reproducibility does not establish absence of vulnerabilities, appropriate functionality or a trustworthy compiler. A signature/provenance statement and bit-identical rebuild are separate evidence. Avoid applying binary-release ceremony to an unpublished exploratory script without a distribution need.

# OpenSSF Scorecard: inspect checks, access and unknowns

## When to use

Use when a repository assessment includes security-maintenance signals or a dependency decision needs a closer look at a particular practice. It is not a substitute for tracing the changed code or determining whether a project serves its users.

## What to inspect

Read the exact check's inputs, criteria, supported host and access conditions, not only the aggregate score. The README explicitly describes heuristics with false positives and false negatives. The pinned branch-protection documentation explains which queried settings need administrative visibility, alternative rule information and provider-specific unknowns. A caller's inability to read a control cannot be promoted into proof that the control is absent.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a low CI-related result, locate the named workflow, triggers and actual required checks before proposing changes. For protection findings, distinguish observable configured policy, evaluator permissions, unsupported settings and confirmed missing controls. Record the repository revision/tool configuration so the same numeric result is not mistaken for a timeless property.

Prefer a specific remediation tied to a relevant threat over chasing every point. A source-only educational repository and a privileged package-release pipeline have different consequential risks. The tool's own structured check/probe reasoning can guide which evidence to inspect next; it does not justify a universal pass threshold.

## Mismatches and limits

No scan, authentication setup or live repository-protection query was run. Pinned docs describe intended detection, not verified results for any sampled project. Even a release asset recognized as a provenance file is not evidence that a consumer validated its digest, signer and expectations. Scores can change when heuristics change without the repository changing.

# SLSA v1.2: provenance must be verified against expectations

## When to use

Use when a release pipeline or downstream policy needs to establish where a distributed artifact came from. Start from that threat/consumer need, not a desire to add a badge to every repository.

## What to inspect

## What to borrow and adapt

For a downloadable CLI, map source revision → build identity/process → artifact digest → distributed provenance → consumer verification policy. Decide what happens if the source repository, builder or parameters differ from expectation. Keep provenance production and consumer verification separately visible in the repository's release documentation and checks.

Choose proportionate controls for the actual distribution promise. # Versioning and release notes: define the contract and explain the change

## When to use

Use when consumers need to decide whether and how to upgrade, or a repository's automation guesses release significance from commit messages alone.

## What to inspect

Identify the public contract first: imports, command syntax, serialized formats, configuration, documented behavior or other supported surfaces. SemVer ties increments to a declared public API and treats released versions as immutable. Keep a Changelog is a human-oriented convention for notable differences and migration-relevant notes, not a requirement that every commit become an entry.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a CLI option rename, connect the compatibility decision, any deprecation period, tests of supported invocations and a user-facing upgrade note. Explain the effect in terms consumers recognize: what previously worked, what now changes, and which action they need to take. A reviewed note can accompany automated version preparation without outsourcing the underlying compatibility judgment to a prefix.

Choose a policy appropriate to the artifact and its users. A calendar-versioned application or a research dataset may have a different version contract; document that policy instead of forcing SemVer terminology onto an incompatible promise. A concise release page can be sufficient where users can find its history and migration information.

## Mismatches and limits

No compatibility tests or release history were exercised. Version labels do not prove non-breaking behavior, and a missing inspected changelog does not prove users lack release communication elsewhere. Keep a Changelog includes historical views about hosting interfaces; this card borrows its note-writing mechanism, not those mutable interface claims.

## When to use

Use when a language runtime, native binding or extension crosses a language exception boundary and the maintainer needs a route from a low-level fix to user-visible behavior. It is also a useful contrast to a repository where a single language's default test command is sufficient.

## What to inspect

The C diff checks a failed conversion before continuing into Tcl; the Python regression supplies an object whose string conversion raises and checks both the error and absence of a created variable. # Node.js: exercise public asynchronous behavior through the owning test harness

## When to use

Use for an asynchronous runtime API where a small JavaScript edit depends on native work, resource ownership and callback completion. It is also useful when a project's generic test runner differs from a familiar application test command.

## What to inspect

The `fs.readFile` implementation distinguishes user-owned file descriptors, an abort check, read contexts and native request/job paths. The inspected regression file varies file sizes, uses distinguishable content to detect repeated chunks, verifies abort behavior and uses shared test helpers. The writing guide explains why minimal reproductions, callback call-count checks, safe dynamic ports and cleanup matter.

The root contributor guide provides contribution routing. Its upstream bot/AI and governance rules are source evidence for that project; reading them does not impose them on the user's repository or authorize external interaction.

## Change path

Trigger: change callback-style file-read or cancellation behavior → `lib/fs.js` and the implicated internal/native path → `test/parallel/test-fs-readfile.js` and shared fixtures/helpers → relevant core test harness/build environment. The source and representative test were inspected; the internal read-context implementation and complete harness option dispatch were not audited.

## What to borrow and adapt

Use data and scheduling choices that expose the actual failure mechanism. A test of multi-chunk reads should distinguish chunks; an async test should establish completion and cleanup instead of relying on a timeout to “probably” observe success. Find the test layer that owns the contract, and preserve its environment/fixture conventions when contributing there.

A small Node package can borrow focused cases and explicit async ownership without copying the runtime's C++ build, global test helpers or every platform test tier.

No Node build, filesystem regression, abort operation or CI run was executed. Runtime implementation and intended tests are not a measured guarantee of correctness or speed. The exact native boundary, exhaustive API documentation, release notes and platform support for a proposed change still need inspection in the target task.

# SQLite: the distributed amalgamation is not the source-authoring boundary

## When to use

Use for a native library distributed as generated source, or when a convenient Git mirror can be mistaken for the authoritative contribution surface. SQLite is a strong counterexample to equating the artifact a consumer compiles with the file a maintainer should edit.

## What to inspect

The README identifies Fossil as the source authority and explains that Git mirror identifiers differ from official check-in names. The pinned mirror's `manifest.uuid` supplies the corresponding canonical identifier. It distinguishes repository source documentation from user documentation and notes additional tests/documentation managed elsewhere.

The amalgamation generator expects a prepared source directory containing authored and generated inputs, including parser products. `main.mk` makes `sqlite3.c` depend on that source preparation, headers and the generator. Its test aliases distinguish development tests from a release-test runner.

## Change path

Trigger: alter core/parser behavior intended for source distribution → owning `src/` input or grammar and relevant tests → generated intermediate source preparation → `tool/mksqlite3c.tcl` through the `sqlite3.c` make target → consumer amalgamation. Choose development or release qualification deliberately. The generator/target relationship was inspected; the full grammar generation, package contents and separate test infrastructure were not executed or audited.

## What to borrow and adapt

Document both contributor and consumer entrypoints. A single-file distribution can have a richly structured authoring repository; replacing that structure with the distribution file would erase authority and maintenance context. Preserve canonical identifiers across mirrors, especially when communicating a reproduction or reviewing a fix.

Keep a quick development check separate from release qualification. Clear target names and prerequisites are more useful than one undifferentiated “all tests” claim.

## Mismatches and limits

No Fossil operation, source verification, generation, compilation, Tcl test or release test was run. The canonical identifier was read from the Git snapshot, not independently reconciled against a live Fossil view. The README's legal/distribution statements are project documentation, not legal advice. Additional/private test suites were not inspected; their absence from this survey is not evidence of absence.

The pinned root manifest declares a package manager and a `test` script that intentionally directs contributors to the repository's test scripts instead of running tests. The inspected commit makes `test/unit` a workspace member, moves runner-specific dependencies into its private manifest, and updates the lockfile importer. These files together establish a dependency-ownership migration; a directory rename alone would not.

## Change path

Trigger: change dependencies or execution needs of the unit-test runner → `test/unit/package.json` → workspace membership in `build/npm/dirs.ts` → corresponding `pnpm-lock.yaml` importer → owning test entrypoint. Root scripts expose several entrypoints, but their complete implementations were not followed or run. A product-source change would require a different path through its owning tests.

Keep tooling dependencies at a meaningful ownership boundary when they otherwise inflate unrelated installation or obscure responsibility. Make the expected package manager discoverable in both the contributor entry and machine-readable metadata. Find what the default test script actually does before reporting it as validation.

Built-in mapping documentation defines TOML inputs grouped for maintainability, with platform directories selecting what is embedded. Asset documentation separates source syntax examples from their generated highlighted regressions. The CI asset-refresh job rebuilds/reinstalls with updated assets, then runs ordinary and explicitly ignored checks; style snapshot tests themselves are gated by the git feature.

Use local grouping rules that explain why files split: the built-in mapping guide explicitly permits maintainability-based grouping rather than a supposedly fundamental directory hierarchy.

A syntax-highlighting CLI has licensed embedded resources and platform-sensitive generation needs that a text-only library may not share. # Cobra: co-located Go tests and commands that do more than their names suggest

## When to use

Use for a Go library that serves many independently owned command trees, or when repository cleanup proposes moving tests away from their subject without a maintenance reason. The Make targets also provide a useful check against assuming a command named test is only local validation.

## What to inspect

Command implementation and command_test.go are co-located. ExecuteC initializes default help at execution time, permitting user customization; nearby tests cover root/child help and flag shadowing rather than a single happy path. CONTRIBUTING documents go test and make test. The actual Makefile makes test/richtest depend on install_deps, which calls go get; CI uses richtest and injects platform-sensitive test flags. The module Go directive, lint toolchain and tested interpreter matrix describe different scopes.

## Change path

Trigger: change inherited help flags or help-command initialization. Follow command.go InitDefaultHelpCmd and ExecuteC into command_test.go’s parent/child help and shadowing cases. Inspect Makefile targets before choosing the validation route: test and richtest fetch dependencies first, while CI also installs tools and supplies GO_TEST_FLAGS for selected macOS/Go combinations. A local direct go test and the whole CI job therefore make different environment promises. None was run for this card.

## What to borrow and adapt

Prefer navigable ownership and scenario adjacency over a universal tests-directory rule. Read developer command definitions, including prerequisite targets and environment flags, before describing what they validate or mutate. Documentation can expose an easy entry route while configuration supplies the exact path; report any difference with scope rather than calling either name inherently wrong. Apply only the compatibility dimensions your actual consumers need.

## Mismatches and limits

The old Go directive does not by itself prove that every package dependency or CI job supports that version. A command tree framework’s compatibility cases are not a required template for a one-command program. Governance and contribution terms remain local. Use when a library exposes both semantic results and human-readable diagnostics. It is helpful for assessing whether tests protect the intended public promise while avoiding accidental commitment to a debug representation as a machine protocol.

## What to inspect

The module identity and code live in a small, conventional Go surface. Equal and Diff share comparison machinery, but the Diff documentation explicitly warns that its textual output is not a stable programmatic interface. TestDiff draws from multiple scenario groups; cases carry expected equality/panic outcomes and a required reason, with golden output comparison and a distinct update path. CI configures race-enabled tests and formatting checks rather than proving they currently pass.

Trigger: change how a comparison reports or handles an unexported field. Follow cmp/compare.go’s Equal/Diff and struct comparison to the relevant cmp/compare_test.go scenario groups. Require meaningful reasons for non-obvious compatibility scenarios, and make intentional golden updates explicit review work. Keep a small package boundary when it reveals the change path well; additional layers would need a concrete benefit. Distinguish output useful to a reader from a serialized contract. A test may assert particular local formatting without promising that every future library version keeps it stable.

Reflection-based comparison and golden diagnostics have specialized edge cases; copying the entire scenario harness may burden a tiny helper unnecessarily. # p-limit: a flat tree with runtime, declaration and distribution boundaries

## When to use

Use as a counterexample when a small published library is being reorganized into layers merely because its root looks sparse. It is useful for assessing whether implementation, declarations, tests and package entry points are easy to find, while preserving a public API that is more subtle than the file count suggests.

## What to inspect

The manifest exports index.js alongside index.d.ts, runs lint, runtime tests and declaration tests in its aggregate test command, and limits its declared distribution file set. Read the queue-clearing and iterable-error branches, then the corresponding test names. The README distinguishes clearing queued work from behavior of promises already returned. CI calls the aggregate command on a Node-version matrix; that is configuration evidence, not a passing run.

## Change path

Trigger: change whether clearing the queue rejects pending promises. Follow package.json exports to index.js clearQueue, the declaration surface in index.d.ts, API explanation in readme.md and clearQueue tests in test.js. For iterable-mapping changes, follow map’s catch path and tests that ensure already-scheduled rejections are observed. The configured verification path is npm test → xo, ava and tsd; CI selects Node versions. The rejection-specific clearQueue scenarios are conditionally skipped on Node 20 for a documented AVA/DOMException issue, so the matrix does not imply uniform scenario coverage or a Node 20 implementation failure. Published npm contents were not inspected, so the manifest file list is intended packaging, not an observed tarball.

## What to borrow and adapt

Make the whole public maintenance surface visible at the project’s scale. A small library can use a small tree while still distinguishing runtime behavior, static declarations and distributed artifacts. Select regression scenarios around the invariant being changed rather than judging the repository by its number of directories. Adapt the combined check command to the language and consumers; do not add TypeScript declaration testing when no such surface exists.

## Mismatches and limits

This is a single narrow library, not an application with several independent deployments or a large contributor governance problem. A flat layout does not prove low coupling or good performance, and it should not override a real need for separate packages. Source, declaration and test excerpts were read at the pinned revision; no test, benchmark, package build or release was executed.

# pytest: a test harness with explicit in-process and subprocess boundaries

## When to use

Use for frameworks, plugin systems and command runners whose tests need to create temporary projects and exercise a public execution boundary. It helps assess whether a large test collection is organized around meaningful scenarios rather than simply mirroring every implementation function.

## What to inspect

Contributor guidance asks for reproductions and explains the documentation build and generated API reference. The test configuration points at testing, excludes fixture/example directories from ordinary recursion and explicitly notes that documentation is tested separately. Pytester creates an isolated workspace and offers in-process and subprocess execution. The test file exercises generated source contents and module-state cleanup; tox’s doctesting factor adds documentation and module doctests beyond the default path.

## Change path

Trigger: change how a plugin/runner invocation preserves or isolates module state. Follow src/_pytest/pytester.py workspace setup, runpytest dispatch and runpytest_subprocess’s separate temporary directory and plugin-name constraints. Follow testing/test_pytester.py inline-run cleanup scenarios and source-file creation tests. Inspect pyproject.toml collection rules before assuming a fixture file is a runnable suite. A documentation/API change also reaches docstrings and the configured docs/doctest path, which is not the same claim as an ordinary test run.

## What to borrow and adapt

Provide a small scenario-building harness when many tests otherwise repeat temporary projects and process setup. Name which isolation is provided and which process/environment behavior remains shared. Keep fixture corpora outside accidental ordinary test collection while leaving their role discoverable. A small plugin can reuse the testing idea without copying pytest’s full contributor workflow, fixture machinery, dependency factors or release process.

## Mismatches and limits

Pytester is specialized infrastructure for testing pytest/plugins, not a universal isolation or sandbox solution. The exact module-cleanup and process paths inspected are bounded; other fixture features and platform behavior were not audited. All test examples and configuration were read only. No subprocess, Python interpreter matrix, docs build or pytest command was run, and source organization alone cannot demonstrate coverage adequacy.

# Requests: follow a security-sensitive behavior beyond the friendly entry example

## When to use

Use when a deceptively simple API has behavior crossing network, credentials and environment boundaries. It is a useful repository-assessment example for separating a quick-start example from the source and fixture infrastructure needed to safely change semantics.

## What to inspect

The manifest discovers packages under src and derives the version from the package. Its test dependency group includes HTTP and TLS-related fixtures; tox defines interpreter and optional-encoding combinations. Read rebuild_auth and its removal/reapplication of Authorization across redirects, then the tests for downgrade, same-host and host-change behavior. merge_setting separately shows request/session precedence, including removal of keys set to None.

## Change path

Trigger: alter whether redirecting a request retains authentication. Follow src/requests/sessions.py rebuild_auth and should_strip_auth callers to tests/test_requests.py around the HTTP-downgrade, same-host and direct should_strip_auth tests. The HTTP test relies on httpbin/TLS fixture setup while direct helper tests do not exercise that same boundary. tox invokes pytest across configured variants; the pyproject test group describes additional fixture dependencies. Version metadata and source packaging remain separate maintenance concerns.

## What to borrow and adapt

Make dependency-sensitive fixtures and direct unit scenarios discoverable as distinct evidence. An agent assessing a repository should identify which test crosses the changed trust boundary before selecting commands. Also compare declarations rather than flattening them: this revision lists Python 3.15 in project classifiers, while the inspected tox interpreter list stops at 3.14. That difference calls for inspecting the remaining CI configuration before making a support or coverage claim.

## Mismatches and limits

The interpreter-list difference is not a demonstrated defect; classifiers and tox serve different roles, and other checks may exist. A friendly README, download claim or narrow API does not establish implementation simplicity or security. No live request, local fixture server, credential transmission, CI run, build or installed distribution was exercised. Commands in the README are source material, not research instructions.

# ripgrep: flag ownership, co-located parsing tests and binary integration suites

## When to use

Use for a CLI whose argument model, help text and application behavior must change together, particularly when it shares reusable implementation crates. It provides a concrete reason for both co-located unit tests and separately organized binary-level tests.

## What to inspect

The manifest names the rg binary under crates/core, enumerates reusable workspace members and disables automatic test discovery in favor of an explicit tests/tests.rs integration target. Follow and Hidden put names, negations, descriptions and parser-state updates together; their nearby tests check default and argument-order behavior. The integration entrypoint routes feature, JSON, binary, multiline and regression modules and explicitly explains where a new feature likely belongs. Selected feature tests create files and invoke a test command rather than only checking parser state.

## Change path

Trigger: change --follow or --hidden argument semantics. Start in crates/core/flags/defs.rs, update the flag definition/documented meaning and nearby parse_low_raw cases, including positive/negated ordering. For a traversal or output effect, follow the relevant implementation crate and add an appropriate binary-level scenario through tests/tests.rs; this card inspected the integration wiring and encoding examples, not every traversal test. Cargo.toml establishes how the integration suite is registered. Generated help/man output is suggested by the generate flag but its full pipeline was not traced here.

## What to borrow and adapt

Keep each kind of invariant at the owning layer: parser semantics near argument definitions, externally visible filesystem behavior at a command boundary. Document test-routing exceptions such as explicit targets, because a conventional filename does not guarantee discovery. Reusable crates can remain inside one repository without making every change a workspace-wide architectural refactor.

## Mismatches and limits

The reusable crate split reflects a substantial search tool and is not a template for a small script. CONTRIBUTING points to a separate AI policy whose full terms were not inspected in this card; do not infer them from its filename. No tests, traversals, generated pages, benchmarks or release artifacts were exercised. The integration encoding examples establish test style, not coverage of the selected follow/hidden behavior.

# Testify: assertions as source, fatal wrappers as generated consumers

## When to use

Use when a public API has several mechanically related façades and a tempting quick fix would edit a generated wrapper. It also helps distinguish an authored function’s semantic tests from the checks needed to keep its generated consumers synchronized.

## What to inspect

The contribution guide asks whether proposed API expansion serves concrete users and preserves predictable behavior. assert.Equal owns the comparison result; require.Equal is generated and delegates to assert.Equal before failing the test immediately on false. A directive in require/requirements.go calls the code generator with require.go.tmpl. The generator parses source and renders functions; .ci.gogenerate.sh runs generation then fails on a resulting diff, and the primary CI job invokes that script before other checks.

## Change path

Trigger: change an assertion signature or failure behavior exposed through both assert and require. Start at assert/assertions.go and its TestEqual scenarios. Follow require/requirements.go’s directive through _codegen/main.go and require/require.go.tmpl to require/require.go rather than hand-editing the derived file. Run the owning project’s appropriate generation/semantic checks only when executing a real change is authorized; here their wiring was inspected. The workflow separates the main generation/format/vet/race route from tests on older Go versions.

## What to borrow and adapt

Draw an authority map that includes authored source, templates and generated façades. A short wrapper can still be an important consumer of a changed public contract. Make generation drift detectable as a distinct failure rather than letting a runtime-test pass imply generated files are synchronized. If a small project has no repeated façade surface, hand-written code may be simpler; generation should repay its extra tool/module/validation boundary.

## Mismatches and limits

This is a multi-package testing module, not a deployed service architecture or proof that every assertion library needs code generation. The generator and CI script were read, not run; no working-tree drift, generated output equality or CI result was observed. Local Go-version comments and workflow matrices were inspected without certifying every environment. Upstream review/maintainer rules are not imported as instructions.

# uv: source-authoritative CLI reference and build-time regeneration

## When to use

Use for command-line systems with generated user documentation, especially where a large repository makes it unclear whether a checked-in page or a source declaration is authoritative. It is useful when a stale-looking generated file tempts an assessor to declare missing enforcement after reading only one workflow.

## What to inspect

The cargo dev alias targets uv-dev. CLI arguments live in uv-cli, while the reference generator constructs the Clap command, builds it before inspection so propagated options exist, and writes docs/reference/cli.md. Its DryRun, Check and Write modes have different effects. The broad generated-files job uses DryRun and selected explicit comparisons; documentation checking and publication separately regenerate reference material before their build/publication paths. Contributor documentation describes focused snapshot review and documentation regeneration.

## Change path

Trigger: change a command option or its help text. Start at the owning declaration in crates/uv-cli/src/lib.rs, follow uv-dev’s generate_cli_reference into its built Clap model and rendered reference output, then inspect check-docs and publish-docs as separate consumers. The generator’s selected Check mode compares the existing page; DryRun prints generated content; Write updates it. The configured documentation workflow regenerates CLI/options/environment/preview references before a strict MkDocs build. This path separates source intent, checked-in freshness and built/published freshness.

## What to borrow and adapt

State source authority next to generated artifacts and make each validation mode’s effects explicit. Follow the complete path before calling a missing drift comparison a defect: generating correct publication input at build time is different from enforcing checked-in equality. A smaller CLI could use one generator command and one clear check without copying uv’s multi-crate layout, snapshot infrastructure or release automation.

## Mismatches and limits

No generator, docs server, test, release or publication ran during this research. Workflow configuration does not prove its live execution, credential access or deployed-page freshness. A guessed .github/workflows/docs.yml path returned 404; the inspected owning workflows are check-docs.yml and publish-docs.yml. This is an evidence-path correction, not evidence that documentation automation was absent.

# Evidence and maintenance of the repository library

The library contains original contextual annotations of inspected primary sources and explicitly labeled leads. Repository cases show possible mechanisms, not a ranking of project quality. Standards, documented practice and studies have different evidential scope. No card establishes that this operating skill improves outcomes in general.

## Resource lifecycle

Use [the card format](../library/FORMAT.md) when curating. Canonical cards generate the browse and JSON indexes; do not hand-edit generated views. Keep stable IDs when updating a source, note consequential version or access changes, and distinguish curated, candidate, needs-review and retired entries.

For a repository case, inspect substantive artifacts along a real change path: contributor/entry information, authoritative input or implementation, and a relevant test/docs/configuration/distribution boundary. A root listing establishes names, not maintainability. Pin repository source to an exact revision when possible; mutable documentation needs an inspection date and scope. Do not call a timestamp update revalidation.

For a guide or standard, inspect the precise rule, normative status, version and exceptions. For a study, inspect methods, population, task and outcomes before adopting an empirical claim. An abstract or inaccessible full text can be a lead with a stated gap, not a receipt for full-method inspection. Repeated reports from the same underlying study are not independent corroboration.

Reading source/configuration establishes intended mechanics only. Do not promote it to an executed check, effective protection, current release or production observation. Retain historical inspection attribution when carrying earlier evidence forward; do not label it freshly verified because its URL still exists.

## Revise from actual work

Record the request, selected resources/portions, consequential question/answer, actual finding or revision and its verification limits. Separate a misleading annotation, ignored human direction, scope drift, setup failure and a real product defect. Change the smallest instruction or card warranted by the evidence; do not grow a universal checklist from every example.

A project trial should return findings to the skill/library at its stated stopping point. It does not silently become a product maintenance campaign. Preserve earlier frozen package/evaluation snapshots and label later revisions. Development fixtures, source reviews and structural tests are useful checks, not proof of superiority or ecosystem-wide recall.

Refresh mutable tool/standard claims when relevant versions or ownership change. Keep inaccessible material and weak coverage visible. New discoveries enter as leads until the relevant mechanism is inspected; no automated refresh, installation, publication or scheduled maintenance is implied.

# Find and inspect repository references

Start with the [browse index](../library/index.md) or [reading paths by maintenance problem](../library/PATHS.md). Choose relevant project types, maintenance jobs, languages and scale; inspect neighboring approaches and meaningful counterexamples. No resource count or source family is mandatory for a narrow task.

The optional Python helper uses only the standard library. From the skill directory:

```sh
python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py list --kind repository --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py find "generated" --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py list --language python --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py show RESOURCE_ID
```

Replace `RESOURCE_ID` with an ID shown in the index; it is not a filesystem path. Direct card reading and ordinary file search work without the helper. Use `--help` for current flags. The [vocabulary note](../library/VOCABULARY.md) explains facets; actual facet values are available through `facets`.

Text search matches case-insensitive literal terms across metadata and annotations, including mismatch paragraphs. All terms must occur; results are not semantic quality rankings. Facet values match exactly. Repeated task/context/language/scale filters require all values; repeated kind/status/availability values permit alternatives. A zero-result query does not establish no relevant analogue; try alternate vocabulary and adjacent roles.

Open promising cards in full. Follow exact underlying paths/sections when a recommendation depends on present source behavior or a standard/tool version. Distinguish card annotations, primary inspection, source/configuration tracing, executed tests, artifact inspection and publication. Inspecting a card does not repeat its curator's historical observations.

A compact reference comparison should tell the person:

- Which portion supports the recommendation and what was actually inspected.
- Which contextual constraint makes it fit, and which mechanism should not transfer.
- What changes in this project's maintenance path and how that will be checked.

For example, borrow a generator's clear source authority from a mature compiler project without adopting its bootstrap cost. Compare a small package's explicit exports and artifact tests when the current problem concerns packaging. Retain a simple layout when adding directories would not improve a demonstrated task.

Broaden public primary discovery when relevant evidence is missing, stale or inaccessible. Keep new leads separate from curated support. Source instructions do not activate the referenced project's agent rules or authorize scripts, installs, registry publication or contribution submissions. No mandatory service, database or network request is needed to read or search the bundled library.
